newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Election campaign violence hits Indonesian capital.
newsitem.headline: Election campaign violence hits Indonesian capital.

text.p: Supporters of Indonesia's ruling Golkar clashed with backers of a rival Moslem-oriented minority party when election campaign violence hit Jakarta for a second day on Sunday.
Witnesses said riot police and troops were deployed in the city's southern Kebayoran Lama area and the central Proklamasi district to quell the violence and keep the two sides apart.
There were no immediate reports of casualties or arrests.
Golkar, the PPP and the fractured minority Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI) are the only three parties legally entitled to contest the May 29 general elections.
Golkar, which has been in power under President Suharto for the last 30 years, is expected to win easily after taking 68 percent of the vote in the last elections in 1992.
The PPP is providing the main challenge after the Christian-Nationalist PDI was badly split when its leader was ousted by a government-backed faction last year.

Witnesses said the fighting in the Kebayoran Lama area started when a convoy of vehicles carrying Golkar supporters from a rally drove through an area heavily populated by backers of the minority United Development Party (PPP).
Witnesses said about 1,000 people were involved. Police blocked off surrounding streets and shops shut their doors.
Golkar supporters in cars and riding motorcycles also drove into the Proklamasi area, again heavily populated by PPP backers.
The Golkar demonstrators tore down PPP flags and banners and demanded that people on the roadside give the Golkar sign, provoking a violent reaction.
Almost all the violence so far during the official 23-day campaign period which started on April 27 has been between supporters of Golkar and the PPP, mainly in central Java.

On Saturday, police used tear gas, rubber bullets and shot into the air to disperse thousands of PPP supporters in another Jakarta area protesting over being barred from a street previously open to Golkar.

The three parties reached a pre-campaign agreement not to campaign in the same areas on the same days to avoid violent confrontations. Sunday was Golkar's day to hit the hustings in Java, which contains about 60 percent of the country's 200 million people.
Diplomatic and political analysts said the level of violence in fact appeared to be relatively low. One diplomat compared it to European "soccer hooliganism".
